Surface parking lots could also be a practical location for a high-capacity designated PUDO facility. Many of these issues arise at high-demand PUDO station locations for TNCs, such as at airports, intermodal hubs, and entertainment venues. The efficiency, reliability, and resilience of these PUDO locations are critical to overall system operation. This is evidenced in various fixed-route transit systems as well, where the overall system capacity is often determined more by station operations at the highest-demand stations than by the traditional view of line capacity. The criticality of station operations and the benefits of “parallel-berth” boarding positions have been extensively explored in various ATN simulation studies, the details of which will be discussed in a subsequent edition of the AMD report series. Figure 28 shows the parallel-berth station configuration at a small-vehicle ATN system station in Masdar City, Abu Dhabi, using physical barriers to prevent passengers from accessing the travel way. This type of offline, parallel-berth functionality can also be applied at actively managed curbside PUDO zones. This is seen frequently at high-capacity TNC PUDO zones at airports, where passengers are directed to multiple offline berths where vehicles are waiting for their passengers, without obstructing the flow of other vehicles. Offline or off-roadway station configurations allow a vehicle to dwell indefinitely without impeding the movements of other vehicles in the system (Lott et al. 2022). Parallel-berth offline stations provide additional benefits to passengers. For example, a party that requires additional time to board does not impede the flow of other passengers to and from the station. Offline station configurations with parallel berths also provide synergistic benefits to implement opportunity charging; for example, a vehicle waiting for a passenger can collect additional charge to extend its operational duty cycle. Further, particularly at high-capacity and intermodal stations where ODT may connect with a higher-capacity regional transit service, the pedestrian space through which the passengers pass to gain access to the AVs should be well coordinated with the design of the other modal facilities—including ensuring personal safety, security, and easy wayfinding while in the space.
